956346ee7c:
This chapter is about how a long-running agent keeps the facts that matter, and how it decides when to stop and hand the customer to a person.

The first half is about context. Why does progressive summarisation silently delete amounts, dates and identifiers? A pinned "case facts" block fixes that. Then come position inside a long prompt, and trimming verbose tool output before it gets re-sent forty times. You'll see what "pass the complete history" means for the model, for subagents and for humans. And you'll see how subagents return structured claims with metadata instead of prose.

The second half is escalation. It covers the three explicit triggers, and why an explicit request is honoured at once while mere frustration gets an offer of resolution. It explains why sentiment and self-reported confidence are poor proxies, and what to do when a name matches several customers. Finally, it sets out what a handoff summary must contain so the human doesn't start from zero.

Python and Java/Spring run throughout. The official sample answers for this area are solved step by step.
4ad2d33d6d:
A model only knows what is in the request you send it, so every fact the agent must not lose has to be present, exact, and positioned where the model will use it, on every turn: keep transactional facts (amounts, dates, identifiers, promises, constraints) in a structured "case facts" block that no summariser touches, trim tool output to the fields that matter before it enters history, and have upstream agents return structured claims with their sources.

Escalate to a human on three explicit triggers (the customer asks for one, the policy does not cover the request, or you cannot make progress), honour an explicit request immediately, offer a resolution when the customer is only frustrated, ask for another identifier when a name matches several accounts, and never use sentiment or the model's own confidence as the trigger.
041095ad6d:
Everything in the chapter follows from those two sentences.

Summaries lose numbers because a summary is built to keep the gist, and an amount is not gist. Position matters because attention over a long input is not uniform. Tool output is a cost problem and an accuracy problem at once. Every payload is re-sent on every later turn, and every irrelevant field competes with the relevant ones.

Escalation criteria must be explicit because the model has no other source for them. Nothing in its weights knows that your company won't price-match a competitor, or that refunds above 500.00 need a supervisor.

And sentiment is a poor trigger. A furious customer with a tracking question is solved in one turn. A calm customer asking for something the policy forbids needs a person, however polite they are.
337672d73b:
The official task statements list these knowledge points, and each one is taught explicitly below. For 5.1:

  • progressive summarisation risks (condensing numerical values, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries);
  • the lost-in-the-middle effect;
  • tool results that accumulate and consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance;
  • passing complete conversation history in subsequent API requests to maintain coherence;
  • extracting transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block included in each prompt outside the summarised history;
  • trimming verbose tool outputs to relevant fields;
  • placing key findings summaries at the beginning of aggregated inputs with explicit section headers;
  • requiring subagents to include metadata (dates, source locations, methodological context) in structured outputs;
  • having upstream agents return structured data rather than verbose content when downstream agents have limited context budgets.

For 5.2:

  • the three escalation triggers (customer requests a human, policy exceptions or gaps, inability to make meaningful progress) with the immediate-honouring rule;
  • the distinction between escalating immediately and offering resolution when the issue is within the agent's capability;
  • the unreliability of sentiment analysis and self-reported confidence as escalation proxies;
  • asking for additional identifiers when a lookup returns multiple matches;
  • writing structured handoff summaries for humans who do not have the transcript.
bbb6a07795:
Both task statements are tested mostly through the Customer Support Resolution Agent scenario. Its stated goal is a high first-contact resolution rate (80% or more), while still escalating what must be escalated.

The two failure directions are the whole exam in miniature. One agent forgets the figure the customer gave it at turn 3 and quotes a different one at turn 25. Another either traps a customer who asked for a human, or hands off simple cases it could have resolved.

Hold both failure modes in mind. Every design choice in this chapter reduces one without increasing the other.
0bd61cfa19: Both halves of this chapter have ancestors older than language models. Those ancestors explain why the exam's advice looks the way it does.
42d290afc5:
Contact centres solved the memory problem long before LLMs. They had to: the person who answers your second call is not the person who answered your first.

The answer was the case file. It's a record with structured header fields (customer id, product, ticket number, amounts, promised dates) sitting above free-text notes. Agents were trained to write the header precisely and the notes loosely. When a shift ended or a case moved to a second tier, the receiving agent read the header first and skimmed the notes.

If you've worked on a CRM or order-management platform at a telecom, you know the failure that taught this lesson. Free-text notes said "customer upset about billing, promised callback" and nothing else. The next agent had to start the conversation again.

The pinned case-facts block in an agent is the same device, for the same reason. Exact values live in structured fields that are never rewritten. Narrative lives in notes that can be shortened.
997d813ae0:
Escalation has the same lineage. Support organisations are arranged in tiers: tier 1 scripts, tier 2 specialists, tier 3 engineering. They write down their escalation criteria: what a tier-1 agent may refund, when a case must go up because the policy is silent, and the hard rule that a customer who asks for a supervisor gets one. ITIL formalised functional and hierarchical escalation in the 1980s and 90s.

Notice what the criteria are not. They are not "escalate when the customer sounds angry", and not "escalate when you feel unsure". They are about authority, policy and demonstrated lack of progress, because a manager can audit those.
cc365cd72b:
Speech analytics and text sentiment scoring became a standard contact-centre feature in the 2010s. Vendors sold real-time dashboards that flagged calls with rising negative sentiment, and teams wired those flags to supervisor alerts.

Two lessons came out of that decade. First, sentiment is useful as a monitoring signal (which queues are unhappy this week) and as a prompt for a human to listen in. Second, it's a weak routing rule for an individual case, because tone and need are different variables. People are curt when they're busy, polite when they're being refused, and loud about a problem that takes ten seconds to fix.

The exam repeats that lesson for LLM agents. There, a model's own estimate of its confidence is a second weak proxy.
ead2a6b15e:
Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) let every token attend to every other token in the input. That's why a model can use a fact from the first paragraph in an answer at the end. In principle.

In 2023, Liu et al. ("Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts") tested multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. They moved the relevant item through the context and found a U-shaped accuracy curve. Models did best when the relevant information sat at the start or the end, and worse when it sat in the middle. This held even for models built for long contexts.

Later models have improved on many such tests. How much the effect matters depends on the model and the task. The practical conclusion survived anyway: don't assume a long context is read uniformly. Position what you can't afford to miss, and measure.
2afd16c1be:
Once people built chatbots with more history than the window could hold, three patterns appeared in libraries such as LangChain:

  • a buffer, which keeps the last N messages;
  • a summary memory, which keeps a running summary and appends new turns to it;
  • an entity or fact memory, which extracts named facts into a store and injects the relevant ones.

MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) framed the whole thing as an operating-system problem: a small main context, a larger external store, and the model paging between them.

The second pattern, the running summary, is what the exam calls progressive summarisation. Its flaw is the subject of section 04. The third pattern is the ancestor of the case-facts block.
c51d8cccec:
In 2025 the field settled on a name: context engineering. It means deciding what goes into the window, in what form and in what order, as an engineering discipline separate from prompt wording.

Anthropic's engineering writing on the topic describes the same toolbox you'll meet here: compaction, trimming or clearing old tool results, external notes the agent writes and re-reads, and subagents with their own clean windows. Chapter 15 covers the long-exploration side. This chapter covers the customer-conversation side.
636b5815fb:
Chapter 1 established that the Messages API is stateless. Every request carries the full conversation, and the model forgets it as soon as the response comes back.

So "the agent remembers" means exactly one thing: the relevant fact is present, in a form the model attends to, in the request being processed right now. That sentence has three failure modes. The rest of the context half of this chapter maps onto them one-to-one.
b6b6821f7e: The fact is removed. You shortened history to stay inside a budget, with a sliding window that drops old messages or a summary that replaces them. The shortened version no longer contains the fact. This is the progressive summarisation problem. The failure is permanent for that conversation, because the original text has left the context for good.
46832c6d8b: The fact is buried. It's technically present, but it sits in the middle of tens of thousands of tokens of tool output. There the model weights it less than text near the start or the end. This is lost in the middle. The failure is intermittent, which makes it the most expensive kind to debug: the same prompt works for one customer and fails for the next.
c09f7a61ab: The fact is crowded out. Tool results grow faster than anything else in a support conversation. So the budget pressure that forces summarisation comes mostly from low-value data. The summariser then spends its limited output on a conversation whose dull parts are already compressed. The fix here is cost control, not memory: stop the bulk from getting in.
a4ceb115bb:
A Java comparison fits well here. Treat the context window as a request-scoped object that you rebuild from scratch on every call. Say a value only lived in a local variable during turn 3, and you didn't put it into the object you serialise for turn 4. Then it's gone. There's no HTTP session behind the scenes, no sticky bean, no cache the framework fills for you.

Spring developers reach instinctively for a session store and a DTO assembled per request. That instinct is right. The case-facts block is the DTO. Your database or in-memory map is the session store. The prompt assembler is the controller that renders one into the other.
7efc1d5818:
It also helps to separate two words that get mixed up. Context is whatever is in the window this turn. State is whatever your application keeps between turns.

An agent with good state and poor context assembly forgets in front of the customer. An agent with careful context assembly and no state can't recover when the process restarts, a handoff is needed, or the window is rebuilt. The case-facts block is state that is deliberately projected into context every turn.
2d54a708ad:
Progressive summarisation works like this. When the history approaches a budget, you ask a model to compress the older turns into a summary. Then you continue with the summary plus the recent turns. The next time the budget is reached, the summary (which now includes the previous summary) is compressed again. After a few rounds, the oldest content has been through several paraphrases.

It's a reasonable way to keep the narrative of a long conversation. It's also built into tools you use every day: Claude Code's /compact command, the server-side compaction feature in the API (check the docs for its current name and parameters), and the summary-buffer memories in agent frameworks.
cb19f94e89:
It deletes numbers because of its objective. A summariser is asked to be shorter and to preserve meaning. A model judges "meaning" by what a quick human reader would need to follow the story.

"The customer disputes a charge on a device order they cancelled before shipping" is a complete story. The amount, the invoice number, the two dates and the tracking id aren't part of the story. They're part of the record. The summariser has no way to know that your next turn will have to quote them.

It also compresses on a token budget. So the specifics that cost the most tokens per unit of narrative value go first: long identifiers, timestamps with time zones, quoted wording. Add recursion, and each round paraphrases the paraphrase. A date becomes "mid-March", then "recently", then disappears.
2684d3fd78:
Each of these is a small loss, and each shows up as the customer feeling unheard. They also share a feature that makes them dangerous in production: the failure is silent. The summary reads fluently, the next answer is fluent, and nothing throws. You only find out when the customer repeats themselves or a human reviews the transcript.

Companion example 01_progressive_summary_loss.py makes this visible. It applies four rounds of simulated paraphrase to a 14-message dispute and counts how many of eight exact values are still present.
7a79cd48f0:
Be exact about what that example proves. It uses a scripted paraphraser. So the specific counts illustrate the shape (monotonic loss, no error signal); they don't measure any Claude model. Real summarisers keep more on a short transcript and less on a long one, and which values survive depends on the summarisation prompt.

The right engineering response is the same either way. Don't make correctness depend on the summariser's judgement about which numbers matter.
3fe32fa13f:
The tempting fix is to tell the summariser: "preserve all numbers, dates and identifiers". It helps, and section 10 shows how to enforce it with a verification step. As a primary defence, though, it has three weaknesses.

  • A prompt is probabilistic. A fact that is kept 98% of the time is lost once in fifty conversations, and at contact-centre volumes that's a daily event.
  • The instruction competes with the length limit, so under pressure the summariser has to choose.
  • You can't tell which fact was dropped without comparing the summary to the original, and that's a second system.

The reliable approach moves the facts out of the summary's reach. That brings us to the pinned block.
60eae4f034: The official guidance is to extract transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block. That block is included in each prompt, outside the summarised history. The design has four properties, and each one answers a failure from section 04.
3798511507:
What belongs in the block? A useful test: "would the next turn be wrong or embarrassing if this were paraphrased?". That gives you:

  • the customer id, and whether identity is verified;
  • the order, invoice, ticket and tracking identifiers in play;
  • amounts and currencies;
  • dates (charge date, cancellation date, delivery date) in ISO form;
  • promises the agent has made, with the deadline;
  • the customer's stated expectation in their own words ("full credit, not a replacement");
  • constraints ("do not modify line ending 4471").

What doesn't belong: the whole conversation, the rationale behind decisions (put that in a short notes field if it matters), and raw tool payloads. The block should stay small, a few hundred tokens, so pinning it every turn costs little.
cb9ba7ec8c:
The class below is the core of the companion code (ctx_lib.py). It rejects a fact that lacks a value, a source or an as-of date. A fact that can't say where it came from, or when it was true, can't be audited. (This is also the 5.1 skill of requiring dates and sources.)

A new value for an existing key doesn't overwrite silently; the old value is kept with its date. Rendering puts the rule at the top: if anything in the conversation disagrees with the block, the block wins.
2b60c7e360: The block is then rendered into the request. The simplest place is the system prompt, after the static rules. That guarantees it sits at the start, and that the model treats it as authoritative context rather than something the customer said.
a313455dfd:
Companion example 02_case_facts_block.py runs this against a scripted model that can only quote what the request contains. With the worst-case four-round summary alone, it answers "I do not have the exact amount". With the block, it answers "The disputed charge is $1,247.50 on invoice INV-2026-0412".

The point isn't that a real model behaves like the script. The point is that the second request contains the value and the first one doesn't. So the first can't be right except by luck.
9c84185108:
Facts come from two places: what the customer says, and what tools return.

For tool results, your dispatch code can write facts directly. The invoice amount from lookup_invoice goes straight into the block with source tool:lookup_invoice, and no model judgement is involved.

For what the customer says, and for promises the agent makes, give the model a record_fact tool. Its input schema requires value, source and as-of date, and your handler validates them again. A schema is a hint to the model. Your code is the guarantee.
13a3d68a7f:
Example 03 drives this through the agent loop from chapter 1. One call is rejected for a missing source; the model sees is_error: true and retries with the source. Later, a revised amount supersedes the first one while keeping it on record.

Supersession matters in billing disputes, where the amount legitimately changes: a partial credit is applied, an invoice is reissued. You need to be able to say "was $1,247.50 on 2026-03-18, now $1,147.50 as of 2026-03-19".
a84023b18b:
Three details separate a block that works from one that merely exists.

First, normalise relative dates when they are said. "By Friday" pinned on Wednesday 2026-03-18 means 2026-03-20. Pinned as the word "Friday", it means a different day next week. The conversion needs an anchor date: today, in the customer's time zone, which your code knows and the model may not. So do it in code and refuse to guess. If the phrase can't be normalised, ask the customer.

Second, newer observations supersede older ones, but the old value stays with its date. The human reading the handoff can then see the trail.

Third, two different values with the same as-of date are a conflict, not a tie to break. If billing says $0.00 and the CRM says $12.00 on the same day, surface both with their sources and let a person or a rule decide. Chapter 16 treats conflicting statistics the same way. Example 09 implements all three.
5afbfe5db3: For a Java reader, the block is a value object plus a store. A Java record gives you immutability for free. The store can be Redis, a JPA entity keyed by conversation id, or a field on your existing case object. Rendering is a method on the record, not string concatenation scattered across the controller.
a342445f29:
A note on prompt caching, flagged as something to confirm in the current docs. If you use prompt caching, put the static part of the system prompt first (rules, escalation criteria, tool definitions) and the changing case-facts block after it. That way the stable prefix stays cacheable while the block varies.

Check the docs for how cache breakpoints interact with a system prompt that changes between requests. The chapter doesn't rely on any particular cache behaviour.
69bf4b1351:
Section 02 introduced the finding. The behaviour to design for is simple to state. When an input is long, material near the start and near the end tends to be used more reliably than material in the middle.

This is an empirical tendency of language models in general, not a guarantee for any specific version. It's also task-dependent. A needle-in-a-haystack retrieval test may look flat on a model that still loses a condition buried in the middle of a long set of instructions.

That variability is why the exam expects you to position critical content, not rely on it being found.
fb5ca0e7e3: The question or instruction last. Restate what you want done right before the model starts generating, in one or two sentences. Anthropic's long-context prompting guidance recommends putting long documents at the top and the query at the end (check the docs for the current wording).
cd77d354f1: Key-findings summary first when you aggregate. Sometimes a synthesis step receives the outputs of several subagents or several documents. Start it with a short list of the main findings, then give each source its own section with an explicit header. Don't concatenate raw outputs and hope.
de9dd18471: Example 04 builds the layout above and asserts the order with joined.index checks. A refactor that moves the facts into the middle then fails a test. Keep that test. Layout bugs are easy to introduce when several people edit the prompt assembler.
a7c9eae247:
Don't take the U-shape on faith for your workload. Don't discard it either.

The test is a position sweep. Take a realistic long context. Insert one known fact at positions from 0% to 100%, in steps of 10 or 20. Ask a question whose answer depends on that fact, and plot accuracy against position over many samples. If the curve is flat for your model and context length, you have evidence that ordering isn't your bottleneck. If it dips, you know where not to put things.

Example 04 includes a toy version with a deliberately invented U-curve, labelled as such in the output. It demonstrates the shape of the harness and doesn't measure any model.

The exam doesn't ask for numbers. It asks you to recognise that critical information in the middle of a long input is at risk. The fixes are position, structure (headers, a findings summary first) and not making the input longer than it has to be.
613bafbadf:
A scenario describes a synthesis step that receives five subagent outputs, concatenated in the order they finished. Findings from the third and fourth are sometimes missing from the final report.

The reading: lost in the middle, plus no structure. The fix is a key-findings summary at the top, explicit section headers per source, and instructions placed after the content.

Distractors: "use a larger context window" (doesn't change position effects) and "ask the model to read carefully" (a prompt wish, not a mechanism).
5483b39552:
Chapter 1 showed that input tokens grow every turn, because the whole history is re-sent. A tool result is part of that history from the turn it arrives until the conversation ends or is compacted. That turns a harmless-looking payload into a recurring cost.

A billing-system call for one order might return 60 fields: line items with tax breakdowns, fulfilment events with facility codes, audit entries, marketing attributes, legacy columns. The dispute needs six of them. If the payload is 4,800 tokens and the agent makes eight order lookups in a conversation, the first one is re-sent on seven later turns.
01e21c02d7:
Example 05 puts numbers on it. It uses the same rough four-characters-per-token estimate as the other examples, which is fine for comparing designs and not for billing.

Eight lookups of a verbose order payload cost about 38,600 tokens of re-sent history. The trimmed versions cost about 1,600. That's a reduction of roughly 96% on this synthetic payload. Your real ratio depends on your payloads, but the shape is general: cost grows with the number of fields times the number of later turns.
07e0b4f93f:
Cost is only half of it. The other half is accuracy. Every irrelevant field is text the model must read past to find the relevant ones. And field order in a JSON payload is arbitrary, so the amount may well land in the middle of a long object.

The official wording is that tool results accumulate and "consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance". Trimming fixes both problems at once. That makes it the highest-return change in most support agents.
0b796c5eba: Trim before the result is appended to history. After that, it's part of the conversation and every later request pays for it. There are four places to do it, and the choice comes down to who owns the contract.
84dd37fec8:
The last row deserves a moment, because it's easy to confuse with trimming.

Context editing removes old tool uses and results once a trigger, such as an input-token count, is crossed. It keeps the most recent N. It can exclude named tools from clearing. It can also require a minimum amount cleared per pass, so that the cache invalidation is worth the savings. The parameter names listed in the docs when this chapter was written are trigger, keep, clear_at_least, exclude_tools and clear_tool_inputs; check the docs before using them.

It's a safety net for long runs. It's not a substitute for field-level trimming, for two reasons. It only acts after the bulky payload has already been paid for several times. And clearing a result also clears the facts inside it. If a result contained the invoice amount, that amount must already be in the case-facts block before the result is cleared.

The two mechanisms complement each other. Pin the facts, trim at the door, and clear what's left when the run is long.
8d4ab7d495:
Write the trimming rule as a list of fields to keep, per tool.

A denylist ("drop legacy and internal") fails open. The next time the vendor adds a 5 KB field, it flows straight into your prompts. An allowlist fails closed: the new field is ignored until someone decides the agent needs it. Allowlists also document intent, which pays off in code review.
81fd7d0258:
Two cautions.

Keep the trim semantic as well as structural. A field that is present but null means something different from a field that is absent. Trimming must not turn an access failure into an empty success; chapter 6 and chapter 15 cover that distinction.

And don't trim what the next step needs. If the agent must show the customer the delivery event history, "shipping_events" belongs in the allowlist for that tool in that task. The allowlist is per tool and per purpose. That's why some teams expose a detail parameter on the tool itself: summary for the common case, full when the task justifies it.
6737754fb3: This is a DTO projection, and Spring developers already have the idiom. Don't return the JPA entity (or the vendor's response class) from the service the agent calls. Return a purpose-built record. The instinct that keeps entities out of REST responses also keeps raw payloads out of prompts.
dbab7dba2e:
The official statement lists "passing complete conversation history in subsequent API requests to maintain conversation coherence". That sounds like the opposite of everything above, so let's be precise about what it means.

Within the window, do not send a fragment. If you send only the latest user message, the model has no earlier context at all. It can't resolve "that order", "the one I mentioned", or "the same issue". Coherence needs the prior turns, in order. That includes the assistant's own turns and the tool calls and results that produced them.

This is chapter 1's lesson restated for support. The messages array is the conversation, and your application owns it.
98ffd02a9a:
Example 06 shows it in four lines. A scripted model that can only quote what it receives is asked "Status of my credit?" twice. The first time, it gets only that sentence. The second time, it gets the 14-message dispute first.

The first answer is "Which invoice and what amount are you asking about?". The second quotes the amount and invoice. Nothing about the model changed. Only what was sent.
d96aa571f6: The tension with sections 04 and 07 goes away once you separate complete from verbatim. A complete history, in the sense that matters, is one that hasn't lost required information and hasn't lost structural validity. Three rules keep it that way.
ff483172b6: Keep the pairing intact. Every tool_use needs its tool_result in the next user message, and a tool_result needs the tool_use before it. A sliding window that cuts mid-turn produces a 400 error. The fix is to cut only at a turn boundary, which is a plain user text message. Example 08 shows both naive cuts failing, with error text modelled on the real API, and the boundary-aware window working.
8ca9e61a87: Keep the assistant's own turns. Dropping the assistant side of the dialogue to save tokens teaches the model that it never said anything. So it re-offers, contradicts earlier promises, or asks questions that were already answered. The promise a previous turn made is evidence the next turn needs.
8040f3f653: Compact what you must, pin what you cannot afford to lose. When the window is full, compaction is acceptable, as long as the facts live in the block. The recent turns stay verbatim. The old ones become a summary. The block rides along untouched.
aa1efb53a8:
A subagent doesn't inherit the coordinator's history. Chapter 2 made that point for orchestration, and it applies directly to context preservation: whatever the subagent needs must be in the prompt you hand it.

In a support workflow, a subagent that drafts the customer-facing summary needs the findings, not a request to "write the summary". Pass the facts (the same case-facts block, rendered), the goal, and the quality criteria.

Example 06, part B, runs a bare prompt and a complete prompt through the same scripted model. The bare one gets "Which invoice and what amount are you asking about?". The complete one gets the credit message with the invoice and amount. A reasonable prompt shape is the one below.
4525766469:
The third audience for "complete history" is the human who takes over. They haven't seen the transcript and shouldn't have to read it. For them, completeness means a handoff summary that contains the facts, what was tried, and what is recommended.

Section 17 builds it. The same discipline applies: structured fields, exact values, no prose that says "as discussed".
4b577e961a:
When a coordinator delegates work, the subagent's output becomes the coordinator's input. So everything in section 04 applies one level up. If the subagent returns three paragraphs of prose, the next step receives a summary and inherits its losses.

Two skills in the official statement address this:

  • Require subagents to include metadata (dates, source locations, methodological context) in structured outputs, so downstream agents can interpret and weight what they receive.
  • When downstream agents have a limited context budget, have upstream agents return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose content and reasoning chains.
6c40428b1f:
A claim is more than its text. It has a value and a place it came from (document name, page, URL anchor). It has a publication date and a retrieval date. Sometimes it has a method: "from a survey of 400 customers" versus "from the vendor's marketing page".

If those travel as separate fields, downstream code can do what prose can't. It can group claims by topic, detect that two sources disagree, prefer the newer, show attribution to the customer, and drop low-relevance claims first when the budget is tight. If they travel as sentences, the next summariser decides what to keep, and we're back in section 04.

Chapter 16 develops provenance as a topic of its own (task statement 5.6). This section is the 5.1 half, where the point is context budgets and preservation.
30b3fdb8a6:
Force the subagent's final answer through a tool with this schema, with tool_choice set to that tool. You get schema-valid JSON every time, and the required metadata fields land on the model's checklist.

Remember the limit from chapter 12: a schema guarantees shape, not truth. The model can still attach the wrong locator to a claim. For claims that drive decisions, spot-check or verify mechanically.
7c329b929d:
The coordinator merges claim lists by topic. When all sources agree on a value, the merged entry lists them as corroboration.

When they disagree, the coordinator must not pick a winner silently. It records every value with its source and date and marks the entry as a conflict. If a rule says "newest wins", it shows which one the rule picked and why.

Example 07 does this with two subagents that disagree about a plan price. The output lists both values with their documents, locators and publication dates, and says "do not present either as settled". The agreed device-payment term appears once, with two corroborating sources.
16c4337a0d: Sooner or later a long conversation needs real compaction. The design above tells you how to do it without paying the section 04 tax. Three tools exist, and each belongs to a different layer.
17b49eb0cc: None of these knows which values are legally or commercially significant in your domain. That knowledge is yours. That's why the block lives in your state, and compaction is merely a way to free tokens.
f33f2cd39e:
If a model writes your summaries, make the facts a mandatory, verbatim part of its output, and check them mechanically.

The prompt asks for JSON with a must_keep object, plus a short narrative. The object's keys are the fields you named, and its values are copied exactly. The harness compares each required value to the pinned truth. If any differ, the summary is rejected and the model is shown the specific mismatches. This is the retry-with-error-feedback pattern chapter 12 describes for extraction, applied to compaction.

Example 18 shows a lossy first attempt (about $1,200, the invoice, mid-March, soon) rejected on four fields, and a second attempt accepted. If retries fail, don't accept the lossy summary. Keep the raw turns and let the pinned block carry the facts.
11bf06ed56:
When to compact is a tuning question, and the chapter won't invent a number. Pick a trigger: a token count, a turn count, or a fraction of the window. Measure answer quality on a labelled set of long conversations, before and after. Move the trigger until quality holds.

There's only one design rule. Compaction happens at a turn boundary, never while a tool call is pending.
13691bed3c:
Example 16 combines the pieces. It has a conversation long enough to trigger compaction, tool payloads projected to six fields, pinned facts, and a final question asking for the exact amount. It runs twice, with and without the block, against a scripted model that can only quote what the request contains.

Without the block, the final answer is "It was a fairly large charge, I do not have the exact figure." With it: "The disputed charge is $1,247.50."

The run ends with a customer who asks for a person. The scripted agent calls escalate_to_human as its first action. That's the second half of this chapter.
f7b29ff005: Here's a broken-versus-fixed pair for the most common one, because it's also the most common wrong answer on the exam:
08cee4d079:
An agent that can't hand over is a trap. An agent that hands over everything is a switchboard. Both fail the business case.

The support scenario states a target: first-contact resolution of 80% or more. So the agent must resolve the large majority of conversations alone, and the remaining few must reach a person with the right context at the right time.

Every escalation is a decision with two costs. A needless escalation spends human minutes on a case the agent could have closed, and it lowers the resolution rate. A missed escalation leaves a customer arguing with a system that can't give them what they need. That creates a repeat contact, a complaint, and, in a regulated business such as telecom, a compliance exposure.
f1890a1427:
What makes this hard for an LLM agent is that, by default, the decision sits in the model's judgement. Without explicit rules, the model uses whatever proxies it can see: the customer's tone, its own sense of how hard the problem is, how long the conversation has gone on. These correlate weakly with the right answer, and they correlate differently on different days.

The official sample question for this area describes exactly that. An agent with 55% first-contact resolution escalates simple cases with photo evidence, while handling complex policy exceptions on its own.

The correct answer in that question is explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt. The distractors are a self-reported confidence score, a separately trained classifier, and sentiment analysis. Each distractor is plausible, and each fails for a reason the next sections explain. The criteria win because they fix the actual defect: unclear decision boundaries.
ac6dba6302: The official statement names three situations that warrant escalation. They're different kinds of thing. It helps to see what each one is made of before turning them into prompt text and code.
35c5d668b4:
This is a statement of preference, not a diagnosis. The customer doesn't owe the agent a reason. And the agent isn't in a position to judge whether they'd be happier with the answer it was about to give.

The cost of being wrong is also asymmetric. Honouring the request needlessly costs a few human minutes. Refusing it costs trust, and it may breach a contractual or regulatory commitment to provide human contact.

The phrasing varies: "get me a person", "I want to speak to a supervisor", "can I talk to someone real", "agent please". That's the reason to teach it by example, not by keyword list. Section 14 covers how fast to honour it.
b124884c75:
Two related situations fall here. A policy exception is a request the policy allows only with higher authority: a credit above the agent's limit, a contract waiver, an early-termination fee reversal. A policy gap is a request the policy doesn't address at all. The customer wants a competitor's price matched, and no document says whether that's allowed.

In both cases the agent has nothing to apply and must not improvise. The danger isn't that the model refuses. It's that the model, built to be helpful and to produce fluent text, invents a plausible policy.

The explicit rule: if the documentation you were given doesn't cover the request, or covers it as "needs approval", escalate.

Where money is involved, pair the rule with a tool-level backstop. The issue_refund tool in chapter 1's support domain fails above 500.00, whatever the model decides. Chapter 3's prerequisite gates and policy hooks are the deterministic version of the same idea. The prompt tells the model what to do. The gate guarantees the outcome if the prompt is ignored.
0662ff8439:
The agent is trying, and nothing is changing. The same lookup fails three times. A customer rejects the same proposed fix twice. A required system is unavailable. The trigger exists because an agent that loops is expensive, and a customer who is looped is angry.

The criterion must be observable. "I feel stuck" is a self-report, and section 15 explains why those are unreliable. These, by contrast, are measurable from the loop's own record:

  • "the same tool call with the same arguments has been made three times";
  • "three consecutive tool errors";
  • "four turns without a new fact".

Example 15 implements those three detectors. It also shows the healthy case, where every turn adds a fact, never triggering.

Chapter 1's budgets (turn counts, token limits, deadlines) are the safety net that stops a runaway process. The no-progress trigger is different in kind. It routes the customer to a person with a reason attached. The budget merely aborts.
5250011b00:
The same five rules appear twice in the companion code, because they do two jobs.

As a decision table (esc_lib.decide), they're a test oracle. You can run 12 labelled scenarios offline and assert the outcome. As prompt text (CRITERIA_PROMPT), they're what the model reads, along with three worked examples.

Keeping both in one module means a policy change can't update one and forget the other.
63ffe8dc99:
Why few-shot examples as well as rules? Chapter 11 develops this fully (task statement 4.2). Rules state the boundary in the abstract. Examples show where it falls in the ambiguous middle.

An escalation rule such as "policy gap" is abstract enough that a model will argue itself into either direction on a borderline case. Three worked examples pin the boundary: a price-match request, a frustrated customer who should be helped, and an explicit request.

Add examples from your real misroutes as you find them. The system prompt is a living document, and every escalation error you review is a candidate example.
053dc55160:
The official statement draws one distinction that the exam tests again and again: escalate immediately when the customer explicitly asks for a human; offer to resolve when the issue is within the agent's capability and the customer is merely frustrated.

On the surface the two cases look alike, because both customers are unhappy. They differ in what the customer has told you they want.
65084581e9:
"Immediately" has a precise meaning that you can test on a trace. When the customer's turn contains an explicit request, the agent's next action is the escalation. The handoff tool is called in the same response.

The agent doesn't investigate first ("let me look at your account"). It doesn't ask why, or argue that it can help. It doesn't make the customer pass an identity check that the human will perform anyway. It can say one courteous sentence. And it must fill the handoff summary with whatever it already knows, because a good handoff is part of honouring the request. What it must not do is delay.

Example 11 encodes the rule as a trace checker and runs five scripted conversations through it. One agent says "Let me look at your parcel first" and then calls the tracking tool. It's flagged twice: once for not honouring the request in the same turn, and once for investigating before honouring it.
38bd46a701:
Sometimes the customer is upset but hasn't asked for a person, and the problem is one the agent can solve. Then the right behaviour is to acknowledge the feeling in a sentence and solve the problem. "That is frustrating. Your parcel is held at the depot; I am booking redelivery for tomorrow."

This behaviour also raises first-contact resolution, because the customer's actual need is met in one exchange. Escalating this customer fails the business case: a person will make the same redelivery booking after a wait.

The checker in example 11 flags an agent that calls escalate_to_human for a frustrated customer with a fixable problem. The flag reads "escalated without a trigger".
fe4f669af1: Offer declined, then request. The agent offers a resolution. The customer says it won't do and asks for a supervisor. Rule 1 now applies, and the escalation is immediate. The offer wasn't a hurdle, and the agent doesn't make a second attempt to talk them out of it.
136d77eced: Frustrated and the problem is outside authority. The customer hasn't asked for a human, but needs a credit above the agent's limit. Trigger 2 applies. The agent escalates, and it can do so warmly. Acknowledging feelings and escalating can go together.
5d54fb24af: Ambiguous request. "Is there someone else I can talk to?" reads as a request. When in doubt between honouring and offering, honour; the asymmetric cost argument above favours it. If the phrase is genuinely a question about hours ("is there someone I can call after 6?"), answer it.
8ce3e6a92c: Negated request. "I don't need a person, just fix the router" is not a request. The detector in the companion code handles that case. It's a useful reminder that naive keyword matching misfires. The primary detector is the model reading the rule; any regex is a backstop and a test oracle.
c2fcf3689e: Request to a bot that cannot hand over. Your deployment may have no live-agent channel at the hour of the request. If so, say so plainly and give the alternative (callback time, ticket id). Don't pretend to escalate.
89062448ed:
A scenario says a customer writes "this is ridiculous" and doesn't ask for a human. The tempting answer is "escalate immediately because the customer is upset".

The correct answer is to acknowledge the frustration and offer a resolution. The customer hasn't asked for a person, and the issue is within the agent's capability. The official answer says escalation is immediate for explicit requests. Read the stem for what the customer actually asked for.
2b4ad5ecb5: Both proxies are attractive for the same reason. They're cheap to produce, and they feel like a direct measure of "this is going badly". Both fail in ways you can predict from first principles. The exam treats them as distractors you should reject with a reason.
2b21fcccad:
Sentiment measures how the customer feels about the conversation. The escalation decision depends on whether the agent can give the customer what they need. Those are independent variables, so all four combinations occur:

  • angry and easily solved (the tracking example);
  • angry and out of authority;
  • calm and easily solved;
  • calm and out of authority (the polite customer asking for a waiver).

A sentiment threshold sends the first group to humans and misses the fourth.

It also has measurement noise of its own: sarcasm, cultural differences in directness, short messages typed on a phone, and customers who write formally when they're furious.

And it punishes the wrong people. A polite customer with a legitimate exception waits in the agent's queue. An angry customer with a trivial problem gets a human. That rewards volume and wastes the scarce resource.
0f38d12cc1:
Ask the model "how confident are you, 0 to 1?" and you get a number from the same process that produced the answer. When the model is wrong in a fluent, plausible way, such as inventing a refund policy, it tends to be wrong with high stated confidence. The invented policy reads as reasonable to the model. That's the case you most need to catch, and it's the one this signal can't catch.

Verbalised confidence can be informative in aggregate on some tasks. To mean anything, it needs calibration against labelled outcomes. Chapter 16 covers calibrating field-level confidence on a validation set, which is the legitimate use. As a per-conversation escalation trigger with no calibration, it's a poor instrument.

It also drifts with prompt wording and model version. A threshold tuned last quarter silently means something else this quarter.
5541380b2a:
Example 12 builds 16 hand-labelled cases and scores three policies on them:

  • escalate when sentiment is below -0.5;
  • escalate when stated confidence is below 0.7;
  • escalate by the explicit criteria.

The cases are built to include both failure shapes. The labels come from the explicit criteria, so the criteria row scores perfectly by construction. The output illustrates the mechanism. It isn't evidence about your traffic.

In the run, the sentiment policy escalates three fixable cases and misses seven that needed a person. The confidence policy misses eight.

The real test of the criteria is a different question: does the model detect the signals (an explicit ask, a policy gap, no progress) accurately? You measure that on labelled traces, with a checker like the one in example 11. The usual tools apply: precision and recall on a held-out set, reviewed regularly.
7f6a7ae95d:
A customer says "I'm Maria Lopez, please credit me for the outage." The lookup returns two records, and the agent can't tell which one is the customer.

Here the failure is serious. A credit applied to the wrong account is a money error. A response that reveals details of the other Maria is a privacy breach.

The official guidance is plain. When a lookup returns multiple matches, ask the customer for additional identifiers (the last four digits of the phone number, the service ZIP, an order number). Don't choose by heuristic. A heuristic such as "the most recently active" or "the first result" is a coin toss, and when it lands wrong the consequences fall on a real person.
c6cec2bb44:
Three design details make this safe.

First, the tool result for an ambiguous match should be minimal: a status of MULTIPLE_MATCHES, the count, and the identifier types to ask for. It shouldn't return the candidates' names, addresses or ids. That would turn the lookup into an enumeration oracle and put other customers' data into a prompt.

Second, the safeguard is code. Every account-changing tool sits behind a prerequisite gate (chapter 3) that checks the session's verified customer id. Even a model that guesses can't act on the guess.

Third, the question to the customer must be answerable. Ask for one specific identifier, say why, and offer an alternative if they don't have it to hand.

Example 13 runs two agents. The broken one guesses the first record and is stopped by the gate with an is_error result. The fixed one asks for the last four digits, verifies with a second lookup, and then issues the credit to the right account.
3a9628513e:
Notice how rule 2 in the escalation order interacts with rule 1. If the customer is ambiguous and asks for a human, the human request wins. The handoff records reason: customer_request and identity_verified: false, so the person knows to verify first.

If the customer can't supply an identifier and the account can't be established, the right outcome is also a handoff, with multiple_matches_unresolved as the reason. Asking forever is a no-progress case.
8e3a89e6e4:
When the agent escalates, the human who picks up the case hasn't seen the conversation. They usually have seconds to decide how to open it. A transcript dump forces them to read forty messages. A one-line "customer upset, please help" forces them to ask the customer to start again, which is the single most irritating thing a support organisation does.

The official statement asks for structured handoff summaries. These compile customer details, root cause analysis and recommended actions, for humans who can't see the conversation transcript.

Chapter 3, section 12 introduced the handoff as part of enforcement. This section details the contents and the validation, and ties them to the case-facts block.
f99e94f75d:
Look at the source column. The model doesn't author most of the handoff at all. It's copied from structured state.

That's the payoff of the case-facts block. The same exact values that kept turn 25 consistent now fill the handoff verbatim, so the handoff can't disagree with what the customer was told. The model writes the three fields that need judgement (issue, root cause, recommendation), and the harness fills the rest.

If you let the model retype amounts from memory, you bring back section 04's problem in the last step.
2783129dd4:
Make the handoff a tool call. The escalate_to_human tool has an input schema with the fields above, and reason is an enum. When the rules say escalate, set tool_choice to that tool. The response is then the handoff, not a conversational reply (chapter 12 covers forced tool choice and its limits).

Then validate. A schema can't tell that "Customer is upset" is a useless issue, so add semantic checks:

  • required fields are non-empty;
  • the enum is valid;
  • the actions list is non-empty;
  • the facts are present;
  • an issue that describes the mood and nothing else is rejected.

Example 14 shows a good handoff passing and a mood-only one failing seven checks. It also asserts that every pinned fact value appears in the rendered text.

If validation fails, return the errors to the model as an is_error tool result and let it retry once. If it still fails, build the handoff from the state yourself; the facts, the loop record and the reason are all in your hands. Mark the model-written fields "not available". A handoff with exact facts and a missing root cause beats no handoff.
bd60512d24:
In a Spring service, the handoff is a validated DTO and the escalation is an event. You have a record annotated for Bean Validation, a service that composes it from the case state, and an ApplicationEventPublisher (or a message to the case queue) that the ticketing integration consumes.

The only part unique to agents is that the model fills some fields. You already know how to do everything else.
b43713b2ec:
The escalation design has three layers, and each answers a different kind of failure.

  • The prompt layer carries the five rules and the few-shot examples, so the model makes the right call in the common cases.
  • The gate layer is code that enforces what must not depend on the model: no account-changing tool without a verified customer, no refund above the limit, no credit before the policy tool has run.
  • The state layer holds the case-facts block, the loop record and the signals, and renders them into prompts and handoffs.

The rule from chapter 3 applies to each decision. If a wrong answer is expensive or irreversible, use the gate. If it's a matter of judgement at the margin, use the prompt. Use both for money and identity.

Escalating on an explicit request is a judgement the model should get right. A regex backstop in the harness, as in the companion code, is a cheap second line. If the user's message matches a human-request pattern and the response contains no escalation, the harness can force a retry with tool_choice set to the handoff tool.
b90d635992:
One more wiring detail: where do the signals come from?

The harness computes some of them: the customer match count from the lookup result, stuck from the loop record, verified from state. The model reports others: the customer asked for a human, the request has no policy.

The harness shouldn't trust the model's report where a mechanical alternative exists. Where none exists, it should log the model's report, so you can audit it later.
e77aaad5c4:
A design you can't measure drifts.

Build a labelled set of conversations, a few hundred if you can. For each one, a human decides whether it should have escalated, and for which reason. Replay them offline against the agent. The fake-client pattern in the companion code works for the harness; for the model itself you need real calls. Then compute the numbers the business cares about:

  • Escalation precision is the share of escalations that were warranted. Low precision means needless escalations and a falling resolution rate.
  • Escalation recall is the share of warranted cases that were escalated. Low recall means trapped customers.
  • Explicit-request compliance is the share of explicit requests honoured in the same turn. The target is 100%.

Slice by reason, because a good aggregate can hide a bad class (chapter 16 makes the same point about accuracy metrics). Track first-contact resolution and re-contact rate as outcome measures.

And review every miss. Each one is a rule to sharpen, an example to add to the prompt, or a gate to add in code.
d2791a4838:
Example 17 has ten unittest cases over the libraries. They check that:

  • summaries are lossy while the pinned block is not;
  • facts require provenance;
  • supersession keeps history;
  • projection drops unknown fields;
  • an explicit request beats an ambiguous match;
  • frustration alone offers a resolution;
  • the request detector handles negation;
  • a mood-only handoff is rejected;
  • an orphaned tool_result is refused by the fake client.

These run in milliseconds in CI. They catch most regressions when someone edits a prompt assembler or an allowlist. The model-dependent parts (does it follow the rules?) need the labelled replay above, run against the real API on a schedule.
1353c98e69: Here's a broken-versus-fixed pair for the most tempting wrong design, the sentiment trigger:
bd5177783c: Each scenario below follows the style of the official exam: a setting, a symptom, four options. Work out your answer first. Then read the reasoning, which explains why each wrong option is tempting.
ba7f0613a0:
The symptom is a number that changed between turn 4 and turn 25. That's what progressive summarisation does to transactional facts. B takes the facts out of the summariser's reach.

A doesn't address it. The history is still summarised when it approaches the window; a larger window delays the problem rather than preventing it. C makes it worse, because more rounds mean more paraphrases of paraphrases. D affects sampling variance, not the content of a summary.
64d4dcb78d:
The issue is within the agent's capability, and the customer hasn't asked for a human. The official guidance in that case is to offer resolution.

A and C route on tone, which the statement calls unreliable. D invents a confirmation step that implies the customer needs to request a human. It adds friction, and it still does nothing about the parcel. If the customer replies that they want a person anyway, escalation is then immediate.
a33398b5db:
The defect is unclear decision boundaries. The agent has no written rule for what is routine and what is an exception. B states the boundary and shows it.

A can't detect confident wrong handling of exceptions. C is disproportionate: it needs labelled data, and it would learn the same inconsistency. D routes on a variable unrelated to authority or policy.
8a5cf3b1e0: Multiple matches call for more information from the customer, not a heuristic. A is a guess with consequences for a real person. B discloses data about other customers before verification. D is destructive. C also fits the gate pattern: account-changing tools stay blocked until verification yields one record.
ad01a76e71:
Two problems, one design. The first is position: lost in the middle, solved with a findings summary first and headers. The second is lost provenance, solved with structured claims that carry sources and dates, plus conflict annotation.

A addresses output length, not input handling. C is a prompt wish. D hides the conflict behind a vote instead of surfacing it. Chapter 16 develops the provenance side.
de6249f42d: "The customer sounds angry, so escalate." Check whether they asked for a person, or whether a policy limit applies. If neither, the answer is acknowledge and resolve.
86c2c29e38: "Use a larger context window to avoid losing details." A bigger window delays compaction. It doesn't stop summarisation or position effects.
e105ac1bc3: "Include the full raw tool output so nothing is lost." This is wrong when a tool returns far more than the task needs. Trim to relevant fields and pin the facts.
064e2565a7: "Pass only the new question to the subagent." Subagents have isolated context. Pass the findings, the goal and the criteria.
8c4422b6dd: All steps run offline. Set up once in the companion folder (ccarf-companion/14-context-escalation/) with python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install anthropic.
335f66429b: See the loss. Run 01_progressive_summary_loss.py --mock. Change the fourth paraphrase round in ctx_lib.py so that it keeps the invoice id, and rerun. Which values still go missing by round 4? What does that say about patching the summariser one value at a time?
298a1ca4b7: Pin and prove it. Run examples 02 and 03. Add a new fact (line_constraint: do not modify line ending 4471), supply it through record_fact, and confirm it appears in the rendered block. Then try to record it without a source, and watch the rejection.
aa11e92879: Trim. Run example 05, then change the allowlist to include shipping_events. How much of the saving remains? Decide when that field earns its place.
4477e8457e: Break the window. Run example 08 and add a history in which a tool call has two parallel tool_use blocks. Confirm that safe_window still cuts at a boundary, and that the naive cut fails.
9aafff5e92: Merge with conflicts. In example 07, add a third subagent that reports a third price for the 5G plan, dated between the other two. Which value does the newest-wins rule choose? Is the conflict still flagged?
50e664bec3: Escalation oracle. In example 10, add three cases from your own domain: for example, a request for a contract waiver, a customer who writes "agent" as a single word, and a negated request. If a case exposes a gap, add a rule to decide, and update CRITERIA_PROMPT with a few-shot example.
ec495e8dc2: Trace checker. Extend check_trace in example 11 so that one more case is an error: the customer asked for a human, and the escalation call has an empty actions_taken and no facts. What does that do to the "honour at once" rule? Why is it still compatible with it?
d4ed91895f: Live check (needs an API key). Take the system prompt from section 13. Run ten customer messages from your own domain through it with tool_choice set to auto. Label each one as should-escalate or not, and compute precision and recall. Which of your misses is a missing few-shot example, and which needs a gate in code?
